2039.problem: Existing fake news video detectors fail on emerging events with unseen topics not in training data.
2039.approach: Leverage stable source-domain reference videos to guide test-time adaptation of unstable target-domain instances.
2039.contribution: RADAR framework enables zero-shot test-time adaptation to fake news videos on new topics via retrieval-guided alignment.
2039.bp: Social platforms need to catch deepfakes and manipulated news as they emerge, not just recognize patterns from yesterday. Speed matters because false narratives spread fast, and retraining every day is impractical.
2039.wh: The classic approach trains once, then applies the model forever. But news topics shift (elections, pandemics, celebrity scandals). A model trained only on past topics watches new events slip through undetected. Retraining requires labeled data you don't have yet.
2039.ap: RADAR flips the script: at test time, when a new video arrives, it searches for similar videos already labeled in the source domain. Videos that are 'stable' (high-confidence, low-entropy) become anchors. Unstable new videos align their learned features to these anchors, essentially saying 'you're like this other video, so you should behave similarly.' Pseudo-labels are then refined using the stable neighbors' information.
2039.ww: Stable references act as landmarks. An unstable video drifting toward a fake reference will be pulled toward a real reference instead. The distribution-level matching grounds the adaptation in shared structure, not just surface similarity. Self-training then scales this to the full target batch.
2039.po: In live tests, RADAR catches fake videos on unseen topics with strong margins over baselines. The system adapts on the fly, generating reliable pseudo-labels even when label distribution shifts (imbalanced, rare classes).

2040.problem: Large-scale urban traffic is heterogeneous; production TTE systems miss city-wide dynamics and long-tail scenarios.
2040.approach: Combine link-level spatio-temporal modeling with route-level learning using mixture-of-experts and incremental adaptation.
2040.contribution: MixTTE deployed at DiDi, reducing TTE errors significantly via scalable multi-scale integration and online learning.
2040.bp: Ride-hailing platforms live or die on prediction accuracy. Get ETAs wrong by 5 minutes and riders cancel; supply-demand balance collapses. But cities have millions of road segments and shifting traffic patterns hour to hour.
2040.wh: Route-level models see the big picture (A to B) but miss that a single clogged intersection cascades across a district. Link-level models capture local dynamics but explode in complexity on a million-road network. Inference must stay under 100ms. Existing methods also assume traffic is stationary; it's not—rush hour, weather, accidents rewire the graph constantly.
2040.ap: MixTTE runs two models in parallel. Link-level uses spatio-temporal external attention (a learnable mechanism that attends to relevant roads globally) to capture traffic wave propagation. Routes then combine these link predictions. A mixture-of-experts layer routes each traffic scenario to the expert best suited to it, avoiding one-size-fits-all bottlenecks. An asynchronous incremental learning thread silently retrains on fresh data without interrupting serving.
2040.ww: External attention scales linearly, not quadratically, so millions of roads stay tractable. Mixture-of-experts exploits the insight that rush-hour congestion needs different logic than late-night flow. Incremental learning keeps the model current as distribution shifts.
2040.po: DiDi's real platform reports substantial accuracy gains and stability. The system now reliably handles long-tail cases (rare intersections, unusual weather) and adapts to seasonal shifts without offline retraining cycles.

2041.problem: Deep learning for large deformations in elastic-plastic solids requires high-accuracy data, which is expensive to simulate.
2041.approach: Use fidelity-based learning: train jointly on cheap low-fidelity and expensive high-fidelity simulation data with attention-based cross-fidelity modules.
2041.contribution: FilDeep framework solves quantity-accuracy tradeoff for large deformation problems, demonstrated on stretch-bending application.
2041.bp: Manufacturing—stamping metal, forging, drawing—depends on predicting how material deforms under extreme stress. Simulations must be accurate to avoid costly trial-and-error, but high-fidelity simulations (fine meshes, plasticity) take hours per case.
2041.wh: You can generate cheap low-fidelity data (coarse mesh, linear assumptions) quickly but it misses reality. High-fidelity is accurate but you can only afford a few hundred cases. Standard deep learning wants thousands of high-quality examples. You're stuck between speed and accuracy.
2041.ap: FilDeep trains a neural network on a mix: thousands of fast, approximate simulations plus hundreds of slow, accurate ones. An attention module learns which low-fidelity patterns are trustworthy and which need correction using high-fidelity examples. The network learns to 'read between the lines' of cheap data and trust it where it's proven reliable.
2041.ww: Attention enables fine-grained weighting: 'this geometry pattern looks similar in low-fidelity data I've seen corrected, so I'll adjust.' The network discovers which features of deformation are robust across fidelities (e.g., final shape) vs. brittle (e.g., stress distribution).
2041.po: FilDeep achieves high-fidelity-level accuracy while training on a mixed dataset that's much cheaper to produce than pure high-fidelity. Manufacturers can now use learned models for quick-turn design iteration without per-case simulation.

2042.problem: Psychiatric symptom datasets are scarce; expert labeling is resource-intensive and symptom expression varies widely across users.
2042.approach: Use LLMs to generate synthetic training data with clinical plausibility: expand symptoms into sub-concepts, vary linguistic style, and respect co-occurrence patterns.
2042.contribution: SynSym produces synthetic data that trains models as well as real data, with further gains from real-data fine-tuning.
2042.bp: Mental health is stigmatized and data-scarce. Social media posts revealing depression or anxiety are rare and sensitive. Yet early detection saves lives. Models trained on real data are brittle—they miss novel expressions because the training set was small and uniform.
2042.wh: Expert psychiatrists annotate posts with symptom labels (anhedonia, insomnia, suicidality). It's slow, expensive, and requires ethics clearance. You end up with hundreds of labeled examples, all in English, all from Reddit or Twitter. The model sees 'I can't sleep' as anhedonia but fails on 'everything feels grey' from a poet's account.
2042.ap: SynSym prompts an LLM (instructed with psychiatric knowledge) to expand each symptom into sub-concepts (e.g., 'depression' → 'low motivation', 'negative self-talk', 'sleep disruption'). For each sub-concept, the LLM generates expressions in diverse linguistic styles (formal, colloquial, poetic). It also composes multi-symptom posts respecting clinical co-occurrence (if depression co-occurs with insomnia in real data, synthetic posts mix them similarly).
2042.ww: LLMs implicitly encode linguistic diversity and clinical relationships from their pretraining. Sub-concepts anchor generation to real symptoms (not hallucination). Clinical co-occurrence constraints ground synthetic data in empirical patterns.
2042.po: Trained on pure synthetic data, models match real-data baselines. Real-data fine-tuning then pushes accuracy higher. SynSym democratizes mental-health NLP—research labs without large labeled datasets can now build generalizable detectors.

2043.problem: LLM pre-training data mixing is typically static; online adaptation methods ignore multiple objectives (quality, domain influence, model stability).
2043.approach: Formulate data scheduling as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem with a holistic reward combining data, loss, and model-driven signals.
2043.contribution: HDS reaches comparable final perplexity with 44% fewer tokens on The Pile benchmark using SAC-based adaptive mixing.
2043.bp: Training an LLM costs millions of dollars and months of compute. Every percentage improvement in data efficiency translates to huge savings. But mixing diverse sources (books, code, web, scientific papers) is an art—nobody knows the optimal recipe.
2043.wh: Static data mixing (always 50% books, 30% code, 20% web) ignores how the model changes. Early in training, raw diversity helps; mid-training, you need harder examples; late, polishing trumps breadth. A single reward objective (e.g., 'minimize loss') ignores that low-quality data can poison multi-lingual or code performance even if average loss looks good.
2043.ap: HDS models data scheduling as a reinforcement learning agent controlling source weights at each step. The Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm balances exploration (try weird mixtures) and exploitation (stick with what works). The reward function combines three signals: (1) a quality score from a data-classifier, (2) a loss-driven signal measuring inter-domain influence (does adding code help or hurt text performance?), and (3) a model-driven signal from weight norms (is the model becoming unbalanced?).
2043.ww: Multi-objective rewards prevent gaming—optimizing purely for loss might sacrifice generalization. SAC's entropy regularization ensures stable exploration without wild swings in mixing ratios. The continuous control space (any mixture is valid, not discrete buckets) lets fine-grained adaptation.
2043.po: On The Pile, HDS reaches the final perplexity of the next-best method using 44% fewer tokens—a dramatic efficiency gain. The agent discovers adaptive schedules (e.g., ramping code in middle training) that humans wouldn't intuit.

2044.problem: IMU sensor data (accelerometer, gyroscope) is hard to interpret for language models; manual IMU-text alignment is impractical due to semantic gap.
2044.approach: Use cross-modal contrastive learning (anchored by vision) offline, then retrieval-augmented generation online to bridge IMU and language.
2044.contribution: Vistar improves IMU-to-text retrieval by up to 57.45% over baselines via aligned multimodal encoders.
2044.bp: Smartphones and robots have inertial sensors. Understanding motion from IMU (is the phone being shaken? is the robot falling?) in natural language lets models reason about physical states without cameras. But IMU is abstract numbers; language is concrete.
2044.wh: You can label videos with text ('person walking upstairs'). You can record IMU during those videos. But the alignment is loose: a 'walking' label spans 3 seconds while IMU oscillates 100 times. It's unclear which frequencies or patterns in the IMU correspond to 'walking' vs. 'ascending.' Humans find this tedious and inconsistent.
2044.ap: Vistar treats vision as a bridge. Offline: encode video frames (with a pretrained vision model) and text ('person walking') jointly; separately, encode the paired IMU signal. A contrastive loss (e.g., SimCLR-style) pulls IMU encoders closer to matching video-text pairs. Hierarchical matching ensures both global events and fine-grained motions align. At test time, given a new IMU signal and a candidate text, Vistar retrieves similar (IMU, text) pairs from a database, re-ranking them structurally (do their IMU patterns match?) and using them to refine the generated description.
2044.ww: Vision models are pretrained on billions of images—they 'understand' motion semantics. By anchoring IMU to pretrained vision, the framework leverages that knowledge without manual labels. Retrieval-augmented generation handles residual misalignment by seeing analogous examples.
2044.po: Models fine-tuned on Vistar embeddings accurately retrieve text descriptions for unseen IMU sequences. The 57.45% improvement shows the framework closes the semantic gap, enabling LLMs to reason about sensor data from smartphones, wearables, and robots.

2045.problem: Operational systems need fast retrospective analysis of high-dimensional timeseries with metadata (QoE, user location, device); traditional data platforms are inefficient or inaccurate.
2045.approach: Build AHA, a specialized system exploiting decomposability, sparsity, and modern database efficiency to enable cost-effective, accurate alternative-history queries.
2045.contribution: AHA reduces operational cost and guarantees fidelity for alternative-history analysis on production timeseries data.
2045.bp: ISPs and CDNs monitor quality metrics for millions of user sessions. When something breaks, engineers ask 'what if we had applied algorithm X to the data from last week?' Replaying historical data through new anomaly detectors or alerting logic is common, but existing tools are slow or imprecise.
2045.wh: Traditional warehouses store raw sessions (10B+ rows, TB+ data). Replaying new logic means scanning all history, which is expensive. Sampling misses rare anomalies. Sketches (e.g., HyperLogLog) are fast but aren't designed for this use case. You can't efficiently answer 'what alerts would algorithm X have fired, grouped by user location?'
2045.ap: AHA redesigns the storage and aggregation layer around alternative-history workloads. Key insights: (1) aggregations decompose—e.g., 'sum(revenue by location)' can be broken into independent sub-sums, (2) only a few attribute-value combinations are active (e.g., most locations see few sessions), and (3) modern columnar DBs (like Clickhouse) are very efficient at filtering by attribute. AHA pre-computes and caches decomposed statistics, marks sparsity (which sub-populations matter), and routes queries to specialized fast-path logic when possible.
2045.ww: Decomposability eliminates redundant computation. Sparsity means you only reprocess sessions from the active sub-populations (e.g., 5 countries, not 200). Columnar storage makes filtering-heavy queries (where device='iPhone' AND location='NYC') very fast because it only reads relevant columns.
2045.po: AHA serves complex alternative-history queries in seconds with full fidelity, not approximations. Engineers can experiment with multiple alert-logic variants retroactively, reducing bugs and improving confidence in deployments.

2046.problem: Deploying LLMs for online QA is latency-sensitive and must handle both simple and complex queries while maintaining consistent reasoning over noisy retrieval context.
2046.approach: Route simple queries to fast direct inference; handle complex queries via iterative reasoning with a long-short memory mechanism and supervised document validation.
2046.contribution: R2R framework adapts computation dynamically, achieving latency-accuracy tradeoff via query difficulty routing and memory-guided reasoning.
2046.bp: Real-world QA (customer support, search, knowledge bases) demands sub-second latency and high accuracy. Not all questions are equal: 'what is 2+2' needs instant reply; 'how do I troubleshoot a rare printer error?' needs careful reasoning with multiple document checks.
2046.wh: Using a single approach fails: pure LLM (fast but hallucinates) and full retrieval+reasoning (accurate but slow). Retrieved documents are often noisy or contradictory. If a document says 'printer model X has 64MB RAM' in one place and '128MB' elsewhere, the model gets confused. Consistency degrades over time.
2046.ap: R2R deploys a Query Critic Agent (QCA) that rates query difficulty by analyzing it without full reasoning. Simple queries bypass retrieval; the LLM answers directly (fast). Complex queries trigger a Memory Augmented Agent (MAA) that iterates: (1) formulate a question based on long-term memory (stable facts) and short-term memory (current knowledge gaps), (2) retrieve documents, (3) a Supervised Retrospection module re-scores retrieved documents against the long-term facts, filtering contradictions, (4) update both memories and repeat until confident.
2046.ww: Long-term memory anchors reasoning in facts established early—if the printer has 64MB, trust that unless overwhelming evidence contradicts. Short-term memory tracks 'what do we still need to know' without noise. The critic agent's routing avoids unnecessary compute on simple queries. Document validation prevents contradictions from poisoning reasoning chains.
2046.po: R2R cuts latency for 70% of queries (simple cases) while maintaining 95%+ accuracy on complex queries via grounded iteration. Live chat systems report better user satisfaction due to faster simple answers and more confident complex answers.

2047.problem: Training GNNs on billion-node graphs using external storage (NVMe SSDs) is I/O-bottlenecked by small random accesses, limiting throughput.
2047.approach: Use block-wise I/O processing and hyperbatch-based minibatching to amortize overhead and fully utilize storage bandwidth.
2047.contribution: AGNES achieves up to 4.1× speedup over state-of-the-art storage-based GNN training via I/O-aware batch scheduling.
2047.bp: Social networks, recommendation graphs, and knowledge bases have billions of nodes and edges. Fitting them in GPU memory is impossible; distributed training is complex. Storage-based training (loading subgraphs from NVMe SSD) is a practical middle ground, but many small I/O requests kill throughput.
2047.wh: Naive batch sampling: for each batch, sample K nodes and fetch their neighborhoods from disk. K small reads (one per node) means the disk barely uses its 5GB/s bandwidth (seek time dominates). You get 100MB/s effective throughput, wasting 95% of hardware potential.
2047.ap: AGNES batches I/O requests: instead of fetching neighborhoods for one batch at a time, it buffers many minibatches and issues one large read request for all their neighborhood data together. For example, if 100 minibatches each need neighborhoods, combine into one 1GB read instead of 10,000 tiny reads. Hyperbatch processing: the batching structure respects graph properties—e.g., if a subgraph fits exactly in L3 cache, use that hyperbatch size to avoid cache misses.
2047.ww: Large sequential I/Os fill the disk's bandwidth efficiently. Batching amortizes seek overhead. Hyperbatch sizing exploits hardware hierarchy (L3 cache, memory bandwidth, GPU transfer latency), turning worst-case (random access) into near-best-case (sequential) I/O patterns.
2047.po: AGNES trains billion-node GNNs on a single machine with NVMe in hours, not days. The 4.1× speedup opens storage-based training to practitioners without clusters, democratizing large-scale GNN research.

2048.problem: Post-training quantization of LLMs degrades accuracy due to non-uniform activation distributions that violate uniform quantization assumptions.
2048.approach: Apply orthogonal transformations (Householder reflections, Givens rotations) to map non-uniform activations to uniform target distributions, then fine-tune globally.
2048.contribution: RUQuant achieves near-optimal quantization by correcting non-uniformity in activation distributions using principled orthogonal transforms.
2048.bp: LLMs are expensive to run. Quantizing weights and activations from float32 to int8 saves 4× memory and speeds inference by 4×. But it destroys accuracy unless done carefully. Deployment teams need methods that keep LLMs accurate at 1/4 size.
2048.wh: Uniform quantization assumes values fit evenly in a range. But LLM activations cluster near zero with occasional outliers (why attention softmax produces 0.95 and 0.02). Mapping outliers to the same step size as normal values wastes precision. The Lloyd-Max optimality condition says the optimal quantization point should shift toward the bulk of the distribution, but uniform schemes ignore this.
2048.ap: RUQuant: (1) divide activations into blocks (e.g., per transformer layer), (2) for each block, construct orthogonal matrices from Householder and Givens transforms—these rotate the coordinate system without changing magnitudes, (3) apply the rotation to map activations to a new basis where they're more uniformly distributed, (4) quantize in the new basis, (5) fine-tune a global Householder reflection at the output to minimize discrepancies in transformer outputs (comparing float vs. quantized).
2048.ww: Orthogonal transforms preserve information (rotation is invertible) while reshaping the distribution. The Lloyd-Max perspective guarantees this is theoretically sound. Global fine-tuning adapts to cross-layer interactions—the model learns to tolerate small quantization errors in layer 5 if it saves precision in layer 3.
2048.po: RUQuant quantizes LLM layers to int8 with minimal accuracy loss (< 2% perplexity increase), compared to 10-15% for naive schemes. Large models (70B parameters) remain accurate, enabling inference on commodity hardware.

2049.problem: Antibody design lacks generative frameworks for full-atom structures that exploit antigen-specific geometric information for local binding interfaces.
2049.approach: Use flow-matching with equivariant surface encoders to end-to-end design antibodies, leveraging antigen interaction data to refine CDR-H3 and global structure.
2049.contribution: AbFlow generates high-quality antibodies with improved binding affinity by incorporating antigen surface geometry into diffusion-based design.
2049.bp: Antibodies are proteins that bind viruses and bacteria, sparking immune response. Designing new antibodies (for COVID, cancer, rare diseases) takes years and millions in R&D. Generative AI could compress design cycles, but antibodies must be stable (full-atom structure) and bind tightly (paratope docking with antigen epitope).
2049.wh: Prior methods generate antibody sequences or abstract structures without full-atom geometry. They ignore the antigen—design works in a vacuum. When you dock the designed antibody to the target antigen, the paratope (binding region) doesn't fit or clashes sterically. You're starting design from scratch for each antigen.
2049.ap: AbFlow models antibody generation as a flow-matching problem: start from noise, gradually denoise toward a realistic antibody structure over many steps. At each step, an equivariant network (respecting rotation/translation symmetries of 3D geometry) predicts the velocity field (direction of denoising). The network is conditioned on the antigen: it encodes the antigen's surface geometry (atoms, positions, chemical properties) and uses this to guide the antibody structure, especially the CDR-H3 loop (the part that contacts the antigen). Optimal transport ensures the denoising path is smooth.
2049.ww: Flow matching is more stable than diffusion for discrete structures (atoms in space). Equivariance means the network respects 3D geometry—rotations in the antigen don't confuse it. Conditioning on surface geometry biases generation toward configurations that will bind; the network 'sees' where it needs to place atoms to fit the binding pocket.
2049.po: AbFlow designs full-atom antibody structures with improved binding affinity to target antigens. Generated antibodies show superior contact interfaces and maintain global stability. The framework enables rapid exploration of variants for therapeutic targets.
